market_context: United States/Canada; non-lethal reduction of spiders indoors through exclusion, housekeeping, prey reduction and safe removal of isolated spiders.
title: How to Reduce Spiders in the House and Keep Them Out

seo.title: How to Reduce Spiders in the House and Keep Them Out
seo.meta_description: Seal gaps, repair screens, reduce insect prey and hiding places, and remove isolated spiders safely. A completely spider-free property is neither practical nor necessary.
seo.search_intent: Reduce indoor spider presence and prevent entry using exclusion and home-maintenance measures rather than extermination-focused treatment.

excerpt: To reduce spiders indoors, focus on why they find entry, prey and shelter: repair screens, seal gaps, keep vegetation and stored materials away from the foundation, reduce insects attracted by lights and organize quiet storage areas. Isolated spiders can be moved with a cup and card when it is safe to do so. It is neither practical nor necessary to eliminate every spider outdoors.
content_html:
Finding a spider in a corner can make it feel as though the house has a bigger problem, but most spiders that turn up indoors are not looking for people. They are looking for shelter or have simply followed the insects they eat.

University of Minnesota Extension emphasizes two useful points: spiders are beneficial predators, and making a home and its surroundings completely spider-free is not practical. A better goal is to reduce entry and make indoor spaces less attractive.

One spider does not automatically mean an infestation

A hunting spider may wander indoors through a door, window or gap and never establish itself. If sightings are occasional, first note where they occur.

When it is safe and the spider is not a species of concern, place a cup or container over it, slide a stiff card underneath and move it outside without direct handling.

If you cannot identify the spider, do not handle it by hand

Most household spiders are not aggressive and bites are uncommon, but some regions have medically important species.

If you are unsure what you found, keep your distance and seek local identification. A clear photograph taken safely can be more useful than trying to catch an unfamiliar spider.

Look for the route indoors

Inspect torn window screens, door sweeps, pipe penetrations, window frames, garage doors and foundation-level cracks.

Repair or seal those openings with appropriate materials. The same work also reduces entry by insects that spiders feed on.

Vegetation touching the house creates bridges

UMN recommends trimming shrubs and plants that directly contact the building and moving piles of bricks, firewood and debris away from the structure.

The goal is not a bare yard. A modest gap around windows, doors and siding reduces direct routes inside.

Outdoor lighting can attract the spiders' food

Bright lights near doors and windows attract nocturnal insects. Where insects gather, predators naturally follow.

Turn off unnecessary lights, aim fixtures away from entrances where practical and use designs that limit scattered light. This addresses the food chain that keeps spiders close to the building.

Indoor clutter creates quiet shelter

Boxes, paper piles and objects left untouched for months create undisturbed hiding places. Decluttering does not magically repel spiders, but it reduces stable shelter and makes new activity easier to notice.

In garages, basements and storage rooms, use closed containers and keep cardboard from sitting directly on damp floors.

Webs show you where activity is concentrating

A new web appearing repeatedly in the same corner indicates a favorable spot: low disturbance, available insects and perhaps a nearby entry point.

Remove abandoned webs when they are unoccupied and inspect the area. If a spider is present and you want a non-lethal approach, relocate it safely first.

Fewer indoor insects usually means fewer spiders

Check screens, trash areas, ripe fruit, moisture, outdoor lighting and other conditions that draw insects inside. You do not need to eliminate every insect outdoors; the goal is to avoid unnecessary concentrations indoors.

A home with fewer available prey insects is less attractive to many spiders.

Do not turn the yard into a battle zone

UMN notes that spiders in lawns and landscapes are beneficial parts of the ecosystem and does not recommend trying to eradicate them outdoors.

If an outdoor web is not blocking a walkway or a frequently used area, leaving it alone is often the simplest choice.

Broad sprays rarely fix the reason spiders are present

Spraying throughout a house does not repair screens, seal cracks, reduce insects around lights or remove shelter. HOME prioritizes exclusion and environmental changes rather than treatments aimed at killing animals.

If spider numbers are unusually high, identify the species and look for the prey or building condition supporting that activity.

When professional help makes sense

Seek help when many spiders appear persistently, you cannot identify a spider that may be medically important, or activity appears to come from inaccessible structural voids.

High spider numbers can also be a reason to investigate other insects; lots of predators may be telling you there is abundant prey.

A protected home does not have to be hostile

Repair screens, seal entry points, trim vegetation, reduce insects attracted by lighting and organize indoor shelter areas. Then handle occasional individual spiders proportionately.

Reducing spiders works best when the house becomes difficult to enter and uninteresting to stay in, not when you try to remove everything living around it.

faq.question: Why do spiders come inside?
faq.answer: They may wander in accidentally or find shelter and insect prey. Gaps, damaged screens and abundant insects make indoor sightings more likely.

faq.question: How can I remove a spider without killing it?
faq.answer: When it is safe and the spider is not a species of concern, cover it with a cup, slide a card underneath and carry it outside without touching it.

faq.question: Should I get rid of spiders in the yard?
faq.answer: Usually not. Spiders are beneficial predators, and UMN does not recommend trying to eliminate them from lawns and landscapes.

faq.question: Why are there suddenly more spiders in my house?
faq.answer: Check entry points and whether insect numbers have increased. Abundant prey can support more spider activity.
